**Conventions.** Measures take values in $[0,\infty]$. For measurable $\varphi\ge 0$ integrals take values in $[0,\infty]$ and we use freely: (i) the Monotone Convergence Theorem (MCT) for pointwise *nondecreasing* sequences of nonnegative measurable functions; (ii) as a consequence, $\int\sum_n\varphi_n\,d\mu=\sum_n\int\varphi_n\,d\mu$ in $[0,\infty]$ for nonnegative measurable $\varphi_n$ (apply MCT to the partial sums; no rule for real sequences is used, so infinite values cause no trouble); (iii) if $\varphi\ge0$ is measurable and $\int\varphi\,d\mu=0$ then $\mu(\{\varphi>0\})=0$ (since $\mu(\{\varphi>1/m\})\le m\int\varphi\,d\mu=0$ and $\{\varphi>0\}=\bigcup_m\{\varphi>1/m\}$); (iv) changing a function on a $\mu$-null set does not change its integrals. Subtractions are performed only between finite quantities.

**Lemma 0 (sums of measures, restrictions).** If $\rho=\mu+\nu$ then $\int\varphi\,d\rho=\int\varphi\,d\mu+\int\varphi\,d\nu$ for every measurable $\varphi\ge0$; and for $E\in\Sigma$, with $\mu_E(A):=\mu(A\cap E)$, $\int\varphi\,d\mu_E=\int\varphi\mathbf 1_E\,d\mu$. *Proof.* Both identities hold for indicators by definition, hence for nonnegative simple functions by linearity, hence for all measurable $\varphi\ge0$ by MCT applied to a nondecreasing sequence of simple functions converging to $\varphi$. $\square$

---

## Part 1: existence when $\mu,\nu$ are finite

Assume $\mu(X),\nu(X)<\infty$ and $\nu\ll\mu$. Put $\rho=\mu+\nu$, a finite measure, with $\nu\le\rho$ setwise.

**Step 1 (Riesz).** Consider the real Hilbert space $L^2(\rho)$. For $f\in L^2(\rho)$, by Lemma 0 and Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$\int|f|\,d\nu\le\int|f|\,d\rho\le\rho(X)^{1/2}\,\|f\|_{L^2(\rho)}<\infty .$$
So $f\in L^1(\nu)$, and $T(f):=\int f\,d\nu$ is well defined on equivalence classes (if $f=0$ $\rho$-a.e. then $f=0$ $\nu$-a.e., since $\nu\le\rho$), linear, and bounded with $|T f|\le\rho(X)^{1/2}\|f\|_2$. By the Riesz representation theorem there is $h\in L^2(\rho)$, which we take to be a real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable representative, such that
$$\int f\,d\nu=\int fh\,d\rho\qquad\text{for all } f\in L^2(\rho). \tag{1}$$
Since $\rho$ is finite, every bounded measurable $f$ lies in $L^2(\rho)$; in particular $\nu(A)=\int_A h\,d\rho$ for all $A\in\Sigma$.

**Step 2 ($0\le h\le1$).** Let $A=\{h<0\}$. Then $0\le\nu(A)=\int_A h\,d\rho=-\int_A(-h)\,d\rho\le0$, so $\int_A (-h)\,d\rho=0$ with $-h>0$ on $A$; by (iii), $\rho(A)=0$. Let $B=\{h>1\}$. Then $\int_B h\,d\rho=\nu(B)\le\rho(B)=\int_B1\,d\rho<\infty$, and $\int_B h\,d\rho\le \int_B |h|\,d\rho<\infty$, so $\int_B(h-1)\,d\rho\le0$ with $h-1>0$ on $B$; by (iii), $\rho(B)=0$. Redefining $h:=0$ on the $\rho$-null set $A\cup B$ keeps $h$ measurable and, by (iv), keeps (1) valid. Now $0\le h\le1$ everywhere.

**Step 3 (key identity).** Let $f\ge0$ be bounded and measurable. By (1) and Lemma 0 (applied to $fh\ge0$),
$$\int f\,d\nu=\int fh\,d\mu+\int fh\,d\nu,$$
and all three terms are finite (bounded by $\sup f\cdot\rho(X)$). Subtracting,
$$\int f(1-h)\,d\nu=\int fh\,d\mu. \tag{2}$$
Now let $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ be any measurable function and $f_k=\min(f,k)$. Then $f_k(1-h)\uparrow f(1-h)$ and $f_kh\uparrow fh$ pointwise (as $0\le h\le1$), so by MCT (2) holds for all measurable $f\ge0$ (as an identity in $[0,\infty]$).

**Step 4 (the set $Z=\{h=1\}$).** Taking $f=\mathbf 1_Z$ in (2): $0=\int_Z(1-h)\,d\nu=\int_Z h\,d\mu=\mu(Z)$. Thus $\mu(Z)=0$, and by absolute continuity $\nu(Z)=0$.

**Step 5 (the density).** Define $g:X\to[0,\infty)$ by $g=h/(1-h)$ on $X\setminus Z$ and $g=0$ on $Z$; $g$ is measurable and finite-valued since $0\le h<1$ on $X\setminus Z$. Fix $A\in\Sigma$ and $n\ge1$, and apply (2) to $f=\mathbf 1_{A\setminus Z}(1+h+\dots+h^{n-1})\ge0$:
$$\int_{A\setminus Z}(1-h^n)\,d\nu=\int_{A\setminus Z}(h+h^2+\dots+h^n)\,d\mu .$$
On $X\setminus Z$ we have $0\le h<1$, so $1-h^n\uparrow1$ and $h+\dots+h^n\uparrow h/(1-h)=g$ as $n\to\infty$, both nondecreasing in $n$. By MCT on both sides, $\nu(A\setminus Z)=\int_{A\setminus Z}g\,d\mu$. Finally $\nu(A)=\nu(A\setminus Z)+\nu(A\cap Z)=\nu(A\setminus Z)$ and $\int_A g\,d\mu=\int_{A\setminus Z}g\,d\mu$ because $g=0$ on $Z$. Hence
$$\nu(A)=\int_A g\,d\mu\qquad(A\in\Sigma).$$

## Part 2: existence in the $\sigma$-finite case

**Partition.** Choose $P_i,Q_j\in\Sigma$ with $X=\bigcup_iP_i=\bigcup_jQ_j$, $\mu(P_i)<\infty$, $\nu(Q_j)<\infty$. Enumerate the countable family $\{P_i\cap Q_j\}_{i,j}$ as $C_1,C_2,\dots$; they cover $X$ and satisfy $\mu(C_m),\nu(C_m)<\infty$. Set $X_1=C_1$, $X_m=C_m\setminus(C_1\cup\dots\cup C_{m-1})$. Then the $X_m$ are pairwise disjoint, measurable, cover $X$, and $\mu(X_m)\le\mu(C_m)<\infty$, $\nu(X_m)<\infty$.

**Local densities.** For each $m$ let $\mu_m(A)=\mu(A\cap X_m)$, $\nu_m(A)=\nu(A\cap X_m)$: finite measures on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $\nu_m\ll\mu_m$ (if $\mu(A\cap X_m)=0$ then $\nu(A\cap X_m)=0$). By Part 1 there is measurable $g_m:X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\nu_m(A)=\int_Ag_m\,d\mu_m=\int_A g_m\mathbf 1_{X_m}\,d\mu$ (Lemma 0).

**Gluing.** Define $g=\sum_m g_m\mathbf 1_{X_m}$. At each point exactly one term is possibly nonzero, so $g:X\to[0,\infty)$ is finite-valued, and it is measurable as a pointwise limit of finite sums of measurable functions. For $A\in\Sigma$, by countable additivity of $\nu$ and (ii),
$$\nu(A)=\sum_m\nu(A\cap X_m)=\sum_m\int \mathbf 1_A g_m\mathbf 1_{X_m}\,d\mu=\int\sum_m\mathbf 1_A g_m\mathbf 1_{X_m}\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu,$$
all equalities holding in $[0,\infty]$. This proves existence.

---

## Part 3: uniqueness

Let $g_1,g_2:X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $\int_Ag_1\,d\mu=\int_Ag_2\,d\mu=\nu(A)$ for all $A\in\Sigma$. Take the partition $(X_m)$ from Part 2. Fix $m$ and let $B=\{g_1>g_2\}\cap X_m\in\Sigma$. Then
$$\int_Bg_1\,d\mu=\int_Bg_2\,d\mu=\nu(B)\le\nu(X_m)<\infty,$$
so $g_1\mathbf 1_B$ and $g_2\mathbf 1_B$ are $\mu$-integrable, and by linearity of the integral on integrable functions $\int_B(g_1-g_2)\,d\mu=0$. The function $(g_1-g_2)\mathbf 1_B$ is nonnegative, measurable, and strictly positive on $B$, so by (iii) $\mu(B)=0$. By symmetry $\mu(\{g_2>g_1\}\cap X_m)=0$. Hence $\mu(\{g_1\ne g_2\}\cap X_m)=0$ for every $m$, and by countable subadditivity
$$\mu(\{g_1\ne g_2\})\le\sum_m\mu(\{g_1\ne g_2\}\cap X_m)=0 .$$
Thus $g_1=g_2$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. $\blacksquare$
